how_to_use: Each entry is a premise for `factory script "<premise>" --style <style> [--length long]`. `hook` is the required first sentence; `question` is the required last line; `verdict` seeds the end card.

clusters.name: Weddings
clusters.signal: Wedding veto, sibling confessions and 'silenced' speeches are the most-shared AITA topics on TikTok this quarter.

stories.title: I pulled my sister's wedding speech after I read the draft
stories.hook: My sister's wedding speech mentioned my ex by name three times, so I told her she wasn't giving it.
stories.twist: The draft she left open was the joke version she'd written to make me laugh. The real one was about our mum, who died in March. She'd rehearsed it forty times.
stories.question: So. Do I apologise, or was I right to check?
stories.verdict: You were right to read it. You were wrong to decide before you asked.

stories.title: My fiancé gave me a list of three people who can't come to our wedding
stories.hook: My fiancé handed me a list of three people who couldn't come to our wedding. My brother was number one.
stories.twist: Reason given: 'you know what he did in 2019'. I don't. Turns out my brother had lent my fiancé eleven thousand dollars that year and never told me, and my fiancé still hasn't paid it back.
stories.question: Do I tell my brother I know, or do I let my fiancé say it first?
stories.verdict: Your brother's silence was a gift. Your fiancé's list was a cover. Ask about the money.

stories.title: The bride asked me to wear white to her wedding. Then she posted the photos.
stories.hook: A week before my ex's wedding, the bride texted me: wear white, I'm serious.
stories.twist: I did. The photos went up with the caption 'some people'. I still have the text. I posted it under the photo.
stories.question: Petty, or fair?
stories.verdict: She set the trap. You just showed the receipt.

stories.title: I told the DJ to cut my dad's song halfway through
stories.hook: My dad requested a song for our father-daughter dance. It was the song he played the night he left us.
stories.twist: He didn't remember. I did. I let it run for one verse, then had the DJ cut it and start the song my stepdad taught me to drive to.
stories.question: Was that cruel, or was it honest?
stories.verdict: That wasn't a dance. That was a verdict. And you'd waited twenty years to give it.

clusters.name: Money and inheritance
clusters.signal: Unequal inheritance splits are the most-forwarded AITA stories this month, and money angles pull finance-tier ad rates without changing the format.

stories.title: My brother says I should get less of Mum's house because I don't have kids
stories.hook: My brother said my share of Mum's house should be smaller because, and I quote, 'you don't have anyone to leave it to'.
stories.twist: I was the one who moved in for the last three years to nurse her. He visited twice. The will splits it fifty-fifty. He wants seventy-thirty and he's already told his kids the house is theirs.
stories.question: Do I take the fifty and lose my brother, or take the forty and keep him?
stories.verdict: The will already answered him. Take the fifty.

stories.title: Grandma left me the house. She left my four cousins one envelope each.
stories.hook: My grandmother left me the house and left my four cousins one envelope each. Mine had a key in it. Theirs had a reason.
stories.twist: Each envelope was a dated list of every visit they'd missed, in her handwriting. Mine wasn't the biggest gift. Theirs was.
stories.question: Would you have shown them what was in yours?
stories.verdict: She wrote four letters and gave one key. Read the letters first.

stories.title: I found the spreadsheet where my parents tracked my rent. My brother paid nothing.
stories.hook: I paid my parents six hundred a month for four years. Last week I found the spreadsheet. My brother's column said zero.
stories.twist: The spreadsheet had a third column, labelled 'return', with my name and a date next month. They'd been saving it for my deposit.
stories.question: So. Do I ask them about the zero, or pretend I never saw it?
stories.verdict: Ask. Gratitude and a question can share a sentence.

stories.title: I paid off my sister's credit card as a surprise. She stopped speaking to me.
stories.hook: I paid off my sister's nine thousand dollars of credit card debt as a surprise. She hasn't spoken to me since.
stories.twist: The card was in her name, but the debt was her husband's. Paying it off closed the account he'd been hiding, and he found out who did it.
stories.question: Did I help her, or did I take her choice away?
stories.verdict: You paid the bill and blew the cover. Both were hers to do.

clusters.name: Roommates and landlords
clusters.signal: Roommate-boundary stories are outperforming family drama on TikTok storytime accounts right now; our v4 story is in this lane.

stories.title: My roommate started charging me per glass of milk. Then I found the notebook.
stories.hook: My roommate started charging me forty cents a glass for milk. Then I found the notebook.
stories.twist: The notebook went back two years. Every item, every cent, both columns. Mine was long. His was blank. So I started my own notebook, beginning with rent.
stories.question: Do I show him, or do I just move out?
stories.verdict: Show him. A notebook only works when both people can read it.

stories.title: My landlord dropped my rent by 300 a month. The neighbour told me why.
stories.hook: My landlord cut my rent by three hundred dollars with no explanation. Then my neighbour told me what he'd done.
stories.twist: He'd sold the building. The new owner had a clause: any tenant on a below-market lease can't be evicted for five years. He'd protected every one of us and told nobody.
stories.question: Do I tell the new owner I know, or do I keep my mouth shut for five years?
stories.verdict: Say nothing to the owner. Say thank you to the man who lost money on you.

stories.title: My roommate's girlfriend moved in without asking, so I did the same
stories.hook: My roommate's girlfriend moved in without asking. So my brother moved in without asking.
stories.twist: The lease says two occupants. My brother is a lawyer. He brought a copy.
stories.question: Too far, or exactly far enough?
stories.verdict: Two people broke the lease. Only one of them brought a copy.

clusters.name: In-laws and family
clusters.signal: 'Sister-in-law hijacks my event' is the fastest-growing AITA sub-genre on the compilations channels.

stories.title: My sister-in-law announced her pregnancy over my daughter's birthday cake. So I announced my divorce.
stories.hook: My sister-in-law announced her pregnancy over my daughter's birthday cake. So I announced my divorce.
stories.twist: I wasn't getting divorced. I am now. My husband's reaction to the fake announcement was relief.
stories.question: Was I wrong to say it, or was I right to find out?
stories.verdict: You lit a match to make a point. It found gas. That isn't on the match.

stories.title: I came home from hospital to a kitchen my mother-in-law had alphabetised
stories.hook: I came home from hospital to find my kitchen alphabetised and my mother-in-law's handwriting on every jar.
stories.twist: One jar said 'insulin, top shelf'. She'd read my discharge notes. She'd also thrown out every sweet in the house, including the ones my son had been hiding for me.
stories.question: Do I thank her, or do I ask for my kitchen back?
stories.verdict: Thank her for the shelf. Take back the drawers.

stories.title: I told my mum I wasn't coming for Christmas. She sent an invoice.
stories.hook: I told my mum I wasn't coming for Christmas. She replied with an invoice for the last twenty-nine.
stories.twist: It was itemised. Turkeys, presents, the year she drove eleven hours. Total: forty-one thousand. At the bottom, in a different pen: 'paid in full, love mum'. Then a second page.
stories.question: Do I open page two?
stories.verdict: Open it. Anyone who itemises twenty-nine Christmases wants to be read, not paid.

clusters.name: Work and malicious compliance
clusters.signal: Malicious-compliance stories hold attention to the end because the payoff is procedural; they also cross-post to r/MaliciousCompliance and r/antiwork.

stories.title: My manager put 'reply within ten minutes' in my contract. I sent 412 emails on Tuesday.
stories.hook: My manager put 'reply to every email within ten minutes' in my contract. So I sent him four hundred and twelve emails on Tuesday.
stories.twist: Each one was a question I'd normally have answered myself. He replied to nine. HR asked why the contract clause existed. It doesn't anymore.
stories.question: Would you have stopped at a hundred?
stories.verdict: You didn't break the rule. You demonstrated it.

stories.title: I found my own job listed online with a salary 20k higher. So I applied.
stories.hook: I found my own job posted online with a salary twenty thousand dollars higher than mine. So I applied.
stories.twist: I got an interview. With my manager. He didn't recognise the CV until the last line, where I'd written 'currently employed as: this'.
stories.question: Do I take the raise, or take the offer I got the next week from somewhere else?
stories.verdict: Take the one from the company that noticed you before you applied.

stories.title: My boss banned personal calls at my desk, so I took them in his office
stories.hook: My boss banned personal calls at desks. He didn't say anything about his office.
stories.twist: I took my daughter's school calls from his chair for a week. On Friday he asked why she kept calling. I told him. The ban has an exception now, and so does he.
stories.question: Petty, or the only way he was going to listen?
stories.verdict: You didn't take his chair. You took his attention.

clusters.name: Petty revenge
clusters.signal: Petty revenge is the highest-completion story type: the audience stays for the mechanism, not the morality.

stories.title: My neighbour parked across my driveway every day for a year. So I rented it to a tow truck.
stories.hook: My neighbour parked across my driveway every day for a year. So I rented my driveway to a tow truck driver.
stories.twist: He got towed on day one, by the truck that lives in my driveway. He complained to the council. The council asked for the driveway owner. I brought the rental agreement.
stories.question: Would you have given him a warning first?
stories.verdict: A year of parking was the warning.

stories.title: My ex kept my Netflix for two years, so I renamed his profile every week
stories.hook: My ex kept using my Netflix for two years, so I renamed his profile every week.
stories.twist: Week ninety-one, his new girlfriend opened the app on his TV. The profile said 'Still Paying Nothing'. She messaged me. We're friends now. He's paying for his own account.
stories.question: Too petty, or perfectly petty?
stories.verdict: Ninety-one weeks of restraint is not petty. It's patient.

clusters.name: Confessions and reveals
clusters.signal: Confession-text trends are running on TikTok; the format where a message meant for someone else lands with the narrator is the most reliable reveal structure.

stories.title: My mum texted me a message meant for my sister. It started with 'don't tell her, but'.
stories.hook: My mum sent me a text meant for my sister. It was about my wedding, and it started with 'don't tell her, but'.
stories.twist: The rest was: 'I've paid the photographer. She thinks it's your money. Let her thank you.' My sister has been letting me thank her for three years.
stories.question: Do I tell them I know, or do I keep thanking the wrong person?
stories.verdict: Thank both of them. Separately. Word for word.

stories.title: For eight years I told my wife her cooking was perfect. She found the diary.
stories.hook: For eight years I told my wife her cooking was perfect. Last week she found my food diary.
stories.twist: Two hundred entries, each rated out of ten, most of them a four. But the last page was a list titled 'things she made that I'd order in a restaurant'. It was long. She's cooking one a night.
stories.question: Does the last page fix the first two hundred?
stories.verdict: You kept score for eight years. The last page is the only one that counts, and she knows it.

stories.title: I've been the anonymous person paying my friend's coffee tab for a year
stories.hook: For a year I've been paying my friend's coffee tab anonymously. Yesterday she thanked her ex for it.
stories.twist: He took the credit. They're back together. The barista knows it was me.
stories.question: Do I say something, or do I let him keep the credit and her?
stories.verdict: Say nothing to her. Say one sentence to him, and let him decide who tells her.

clusters.name: Relationships
clusters.signal: 'Left my husband at home' and 'told my fiancé the truth about my kid' were the two biggest AITA reposts of the month.

stories.title: I went on our tenth-anniversary trip alone. The hotel had him checked in already.
stories.hook: I went on our tenth-anniversary trip alone because he 'couldn't get the days off'. The hotel had him listed as already checked in.
stories.twist: He was there. With my parents. And a photographer. He'd flown them out to surprise me and got the dates wrong by one day. I'd already messaged the divorce lawyer from the lobby.
stories.question: Do I tell him about the message?
stories.verdict: Tell him. A surprise that starts with a lie earns one honest sentence back.

stories.title: My girlfriend's rule is no phones at dinner. I found out why.
stories.hook: My girlfriend has one rule: no phones at dinner. Last week I found out why.
stories.twist: Her last relationship ended over a text she read across a table. She still has it. She showed me. It was from me, to her, before we met, sent to the wrong number. I'd asked someone else to marry me.
stories.question: So. Do I ask her now, or is that the worst possible moment?
stories.verdict: Not at dinner. Anywhere but dinner.
